Peterloo. The massacre occurred on August 16, 1819, in Manchester, England, when British cavalry and militia charged into a peaceful crowd of 60,000 to 100,000 political reformers. The crowd had gathered to hear orator Henry Hunt speak in support of parliamentary reform and working-class representation. The name was a dark joke by reformers alluding to the Battle of Waterloo, meant to describe what they saw as a military attack on civilians exercising their right of assembly. Between 15 and 18 people died in the immediate aftermath, with dozens more wounded, and the event became a catalyst for the nascent labor and reform movements.

The reform rally took place on St. Peter's Field in Manchester, a manufacturing center with a large working-class population suffering from industrial depression and excluded from political representation. Henry Hunt, a radical orator from London, was invited to address the crowd, and attendees included workers, their families, and supporters of the Hampden Clubs, organizations advocating democratic reform. The assembly was peaceful and orderly, with banners calling for universal suffrage and the repeal of the Corn Laws, and the crowd was entirely unarmed.

Local magistrates, alarmed by the size and political character of the gathering, ordered the cavalry and militia to disperse the crowd and arrest Hunt. Soldiers, many of them inexperienced and nervous, charged the densely packed crowd on horseback with sabres drawn. In the chaos, people were trampled and slashed, women and children were knocked down, and the crowd had limited routes to escape.

The crowd dispersed in panic, and bodies and the wounded were left on the field. The shocking scene was reported in newspapers across Britain. Trials of the organizers resulted in acquittals or light sentences, while the magistrates and military officers faced no prosecution. The government responded with the Six Acts of 1819, repressive legislation targeting public assemblies, seditious speech, and the radical press. Yet Peterloo energized the reform movement rather than suppressing it. The event became a rallying cry for advocates of universal suffrage and workers' rights and was commemorated annually by reformers, becoming a founding myth of the labor movement in Britain. Peterloo contributed to the eventual passage of the Great Reform Act of 1832, which expanded the franchise, and demonstrated that British military and magistrates would use force against peacefully assembled civilians, hardening the conviction among reformers that the system had to be overthrown rather than petitioned.
